clue.text: In which a tell-tale wife came clean?

definitions.text: In which a tell-tale wife came clean?

parts.words: In which a tell-tale wife came clean?
parts.note: the tell-tale wife is Chaucer's Wife of Bath, who tells a tale; the place where one gets clean is read as a vessel named after her city plus a tub

explanation.surface: A gossiping wife finally confessed, and the question is where she did it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came clean' suggests confessing, but here it means washing; the tale-telling wife is Chaucer's Wife of Bath, which points at the first half of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub for bathing is where anyone, including a wife of Bath, gets washed.

clue.text: Note American taking no proper holiday

annotationWithheld.why: Note American taking no proper holiday (6): Note gives B and American US, but no clue word gives MAN, and the rest only defines a busman's holiday; the clue appears incomplete
annotationWithheld.clue: Note American taking no proper holiday

clue.text: Stain hard to sort out? That's about right

definitions.text: Stain hard to sort out? That's about right

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the next piece
to sort something out is to put its letters into a new order

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A stubborn stain is difficult to get rid of, and that seems about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to sort out' rearranges STAIN plus H into TANISH; 'about' puts that round R. The whole clue also describes the answer, a stain not easily removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarnish is the dull discoloration on metal that resists cleaning.

clue.text: One who values highly his position in society?

definitions.text: One who values highly his position in society?

parts.words: One who values highly his position in society?
parts.note: read as someone who treasures things, holding an office in a club or association that looks after the money

explanation.surface: A snob prizes their social standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Values highly' suggests status-consciousness, but it is a playful reading of an officer's title; 'society' is a club, not high society.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer who keeps a society's funds is literally one who treasures.

clue.text: What biographers do to one put on trial

definitions.text: What biographers do to one put on trial

parts.words: What biographers do to one put on trial
parts.note: a biographer turns a life into a printed volume, and the same phrase means calling an offender to account

explanation.surface: Writers turn their attention to a defendant's story.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to make someone answer for misdeeds, and literally describes putting a life into a volume.

clue.text: Fine innings contributed to county total

explanation.surface: A batsman's splendid knock added to his county side's score.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a score of a hundred runs is a century; in English history a hundred was a subdivision of a shire, so hundreds together made up the county.
explanation.definitionFit: A century of runs is a fine innings, and the old administrative districts called hundreds were the parts a shire was divided into.

clue.text: Tool to down for the dance

explanation.surface: Someone sets a garden implement aside to go dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition says the word goes in front of 'down' to make the dance, a hoedown, a lively country dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoe is a gardening implement, and placed before 'down' it forms the name of a barn dance.

clue.text: Bridge player leading diamonds — king would be subtler

indicators.note: leading means the first piece comes in front of the next

parts.note: North, N, is one of the four seats at a bridge table
ice is slang for diamonds
R, from Rex, is the abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A card player leads with a diamond, suggesting a king would be a cleverer lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicer can mean more finely discriminating, as in a nice distinction.

clue.text: Is found in province, not in Spanish castle

indicators.note: found in means the first word is placed inside the second

parts.note: a realm is a province or domain

explanation.surface: A traveller notes something is in one region of Spain but not inside its castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Castles in Spain' are daydreams; the attitude that avoids them is a practical one.
explanation.definitionFit: Realism is a practical outlook, the opposite of building fanciful schemes in the air.

clue.text: Broadcast is hell, intrinsically

parts.note: Dis is the Roman underworld, so hell
per se is Latin for in itself, intrinsically

explanation.surface: Someone declares that broadcasting is hell by its very nature.
explanation.definitionFit: To broadcast seeds is to scatter them widely.

clue.text: Guilty man may, when court proceedings start?

explanation.surface: A convicted man waits for the trial to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'court' is a tennis court, where each point begins with a serve; the guilty man goes to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A convict does a prison sentence, and on a tennis court play opens at the moment of the first serve.

clue.text: Lot of pupils put right for left-so very stupid!

indicators.note: the right-hand letter R is put where the letter for left, L, stood in the word

parts.note: a class is a group of pupils taught together

explanation.surface: A teacher despairs that a whole class keeps mixing up right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Crass describes gross, insensitive stupidity.

clue.text: A state abbreviated wrongly

parts.note: Miss. is the short form of the US state of Mississippi

explanation.surface: Someone shortens the name of a state incorrectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiss is an adverb for going astray or being done in error.

clue.text: Bargained wildly for the material

indicators.note: doing something wildly means without order, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A shopper haggled furiously over a length of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabardine is a firm twill fabric used for raincoats.

clue.text: Clue number for twelve, here in London?

definitions.text: Clue number for twelve, here in London?

parts.words: Clue number for twelve, here in London?
parts.note: this clue is numbered 13, a baker's dozen, which a baker gives for twelve; it also names a London road

explanation.surface: A puzzled solver asks which clue number stands for twelve somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: A baker's dozen is thirteen, the clue's own number; the London street is the fictional home of the detective in 14 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The London thoroughfare is famous as the address of Conan Doyle's detective, and its first word recalls a baker's thirteen.

clue.text: Violinist of 13 who bowed out in 1914

definitions.text: Violinist of 13 who bowed out in 1914

parts.words: Violinist of 13 who bowed out in 1914
parts.note: Conan Doyle's detective lived at the London address in 13 down and played the violin; His Last Bow, the story of his final case, is set in 1914

explanation.surface: A fiddler from a numbered address gave his farewell performance on the eve of the Great War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowed out' plays on a violinist's bow and on retiring, echoing the story title His Last Bow.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional sleuth was an amateur violinist whose last recorded adventure takes place in August 1914.

clue.text: Attack on the way — what's funny in that?

indicators.note: in means what's funny is placed inside the abbreviation for the way

parts.note: ST, street, is a way
a laugh is what something funny produces

explanation.surface: A heckler asks what is so amusing while out on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: An onslaught is a fierce assault.

clue.text: Sentimentality given scope to spread rapidly

parts.note: mush is soppy sentimentality
room means scope or space to act

explanation.surface: Gushing feeling, given freedom, quickly takes over.
explanation.definitionFit: To mushroom is to grow or expand suddenly, like fungi overnight.

clue.text: Starving after change in hour dinner's due

indicators.note: a change in these words means their letters are rearranged into another order

explanation.surface: Someone is famished because the dinner hour has been moved later.
explanation.definitionFit: Being undernourished means lacking enough food, as one starving does.

clue.text: Simple song without a point

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the song goes around the other letters

parts.note: a ditty is a simple song
N, north, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A basic tune that doesn't really have a purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple' is the old noun for a medicinal herb, not an adjective; 'without' means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Dittany is an aromatic herb once used medicinally, and such plants were called simples.

clue.text: I'm a high-flier, say — not a pretty sight

indicators.note: say means the phrase is spoken and the sound gives the answer

parts.note: a high flier could boast 'I soar'

explanation.surface: A boastful high achiever is told they look unattractive.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something ugly to look at.

clue.text: Heard on board ship, in cabin

explanation.surface: A sound overheard in a ship's cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: A sea shanty is a sailors' work song; a shanty is also a rough hut.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors sang shanties while working, and the same word means a crude hut.

clue.text: Method of dismissal brings strike at gate

parts.note: to hit is to strike
a wicket is a small gate, often set in a larger one

explanation.surface: A protest in which strikers picket the gates sacks someone.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman is out hit wicket when he knocks over his own stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a batsman dislodging the bails with bat or body is one of the ways of being given out.

clue.text: Get into ground — part of main terrace

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A football fan gets into the stadium and joins the main terrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' is a verb here, put into the ground: to inter is to bury.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury, putting a body in the earth.

clue.text: First letter from Herbert about the French

indicators.note: about means the initials surround the French article, placed within them

parts.note: the humorist A.P. Herbert signed his Punch pieces with his initials, APH
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: An early letter arrives from a man called Herbert, concerning the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleph begins the Hebrew alphabet.

clue.text: This sort of painting means nothing to some

parts.note: O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing
part means some of a whole

explanation.surface: A dismissive critic says a kind of picture means nothing to certain people.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is the 1960s style of abstract painting that uses optical illusion.

clue.text: Finished with wrong change, certainly not 17

parts.note: over means finished or ended

indicators.note: a change to the word wrong means its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is done with getting the wrong coins back.
explanation.walkthrough: '17' points to the starving answer; something overgrown has grown too much, the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Being overgrown means having grown excessively, far from going short of food.

clue.text: Baker's daughter needlessly sent to Athens

explanation.surface: A tradesman's daughter is sent off to Greece for no good reason.
explanation.walkthrough: Ophelia in Hamlet says the owl was a baker's daughter, from a legend; sending owls to Athens, city of the owl-emblemed Athena, means a pointless act.
explanation.definitionFit: In folk legend a baker's daughter was turned into the night bird, and taking such birds to Athens was a proverb for superfluous effort.

clue.text: Like Henchard's position in spring exam

parts.note: May is a month of spring
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A student's standing depends on a test taken in the spring.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Henchard is the title character of Thomas Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Henchard held civic office as head of the town council, so his post was that of its chief citizen.

clue.text: Far from stable, yet trot all over the place

indicators.note: letters scattered all over the place are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A horse is unsteady, yet it still trots about everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Tottery describes something shaky and liable to fall.
